title: What is well planted
hookLine: what is well planted can't be uprooted; cultivate it in yourself, then your home and village (Tao Te Ching 54)
carry: cultivate it in yourself, and it spreads
last: SPLENDOR THAT STARVES THE FIELDS IS THEFT.

cards: The morning after a big storm, a street looks like a sorting machine went through it. The young ornamental tree out front, the one that looked so tidy, is lying across the sidewalk with a flat pad of roots in the air.
Two doors down, an old tree has lost some branches and is otherwise exactly where it was. Same wind. Same night.
The difference was underground, where nobody was looking. Chapter fifty-four of the Tao Te Ching is about that underground difference, and how far it can reach.

teach.h: WHAT IS WELL PLANTED ISN'T UPROOTED.
teach.b: First, the planting. James Legge set this chapter as verse, and it opens: "What (Tao's) skilful planter plants can never be uptorn."
What is held well, it goes on, won't slip away, and the family's offerings carry on from one generation to the next. Rootedness isn't only about surviving a storm. It's about lasting.
Second, the circles. Cultivate it in yourself, the chapter says, and your virtue becomes real. In your family, it overflows.
In your village, it endures. In the state, it flourishes. In the whole world, it spreads everywhere.
It doesn't start with the world. It starts with one person, and moves out like rings in a pond. Third, the method.
Look at a person by way of a person, a family by way of a family, a village by way of a village, the world by way of the world. How do I know the world is like this, the speaker asks. By this.

teach.h: LOOK AT EACH SIZE AS IT IS.
teach.b: Look at what's actually there, at each size, and see whether the roots hold. Fourth, a smaller garden.
Good intentions often get planted shallow: a resolution on a sticky note, a burst of effort that looks tidy for a week. The first strong wind takes it. The chapter's picture is slower.
One good thing, put down deep in one life, until it's there whether or not anyone is watching.
Then, without any campaign, it starts showing up at the kitchen table, and then down the street.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter fifty-four as a teaching that change begins in one's own life and widens to family, village and world, and that only what is deeply rooted lasts.

o: a seed sown in the right season of the year
rooted so deep that nothing can pull it up
a habit started with a big, bold burst of effort

s: chapter fifty-four starts with changing the world
it starts with cultivating it in yourself, then family, village, state and world.
the chapter says what is well planted can't be uprooted
Legge sets it as verse: what the skilful planter plants can never be uptorn.
the chapter says to judge every size by the same yardstick
it says to look at a person as a person, a family as a family, and so on up to the world.

games.q: you want something good to spread through your neighborhood. where does chapter fifty-four say to start?
o: with a petition to the whole town.
with whoever is doing the most harm.
games.why: the chapter starts with cultivating it in yourself, then moves out to the family, the village, the state and the world.

practice: Don't reach for a new habit; pick one good thing you already do, even a little, like a walk, a kind word at dinner, or a few minutes of quiet like this one.

Picture it as a young tree, and ask what would put its roots one inch deeper: the same time each day, a smaller, steadier version, doing it on the days you don't feel like it. Choose one inch, and rest with that choice.

wordCard.voice: Well planted. Chapter fifty-four: what is planted well can't be pulled up, and it grows outward from one person to a family, a village and the world. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: what is well established is not pulled up, the opening of chapter fifty-four.

carryVoice: Your line: cultivate it in yourself, and it spreads. Self, family, village, world; and what's rooted deep is still standing the morning after. See you tomorrow.
